author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify the structural components of DNA — the sugar-phosphate backbone, the four nitrogenous bases, and the hydrogen bonds between base pairs — and describe how they assemble into the double helix.

Students will apply the complementary base-pairing rules (A with T, G with C) to determine the sequence of one strand given the sequence of the other, and explain why these specific pairings occur (two hydrogen bonds for A-T, three for G-C).
Students will describe the antiparallel orientation of the two strands of DNA and explain how the 5'-to-3' directionality of each sugar-phosphate backbone determines this arrangement.
Students will trace the action of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork, identifying which enzyme performs which function.

Students will explain why DNA replication produces a leading strand synthesized continuously and a lagging strand synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, relating this asymmetry to the unidirectional 5'-to-3' activity of DNA polymerase on antiparallel templates.
Students will articulate why DNA replication is described as semiconservative, and predict the composition of daughter molecules after one and two rounds of replication.

modules.description: Examine a simplified, flat schematic representation of the DNA double helix to understand its core repeating components: backbones and base pairs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the sugar-phosphate backbone and its role as the structural support of DNA.
Recognize the four nitrogenous bases (A, T, G, C) and their complementary nature in a simplified visual model.
instructions: Examine the flat schematic ladder. Notice the repeating sugar-phosphate backbone and the color-coded base pairings.
Observe the letter labels (A, T, G, C) representing each nitrogenous base on the rungs.

components.text: DNA is a polymer made of two complementary strands. In this simplified ladder view, the vertical poles are the sugar-phosphate backbones, and the horizontal rungs represent nitrogenous base pairs projecting inward.

clips.changeMeaning: The lab begins by spawning the schematic ladder representation of DNA along with introductory text.
clips.narration: Welcome to the study of DNA structure and replication. We begin with a simplified schematic ladder representation of DNA. The two vertical columns represent the sugar-phosphate backbones, which run in opposite directions. The horizontal rungs represent complementary nitrogenous bases projecting inward. Adenine in red pairs with Thymine in blue, and Guanine in yellow pairs with Cytosine in green. This regular arrangement forms the core blueprint of life.

modules.description: Transition the schematic ladder into a realistic 3D rotating double-helix structure to build mental mapping of real DNA geometry.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe how a flat DNA structure twists to form the three-dimensional double helix.
Observe how nitrogenous base pairs stack flat in the interior of the double helix.
Identify the helical pitch, noting that DNA completes one full rotation roughly every 10 base pairs.
instructions: Watch the transition as the flat ladder morphs or switches to the 3D rotating double helix.
Observe the spatial stacking of the complementary base pairs along the interior axis.

components.text: Watch how the flat schematic ladder twists into the 3D double helix. The backbones spiral around a central axis, with base pairs stacking neatly on the interior. Real DNA completes one full turn approximately every 10 base pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: The flat ladder is hidden and the realistic rotating double helix is revealed to demonstrate structural transition.
clips.narration: In a cell, DNA doesn't remain flat. Watch as the ladder twists around a common central axis, forming the famous double helix. Notice how the backbones spiral on the outside, shielding the base pairs stacked on the inside. This helical turn occurs every ten base pairs, creating alternating major and minor grooves in its structural landscape.

modules.description: Examine the antiparallel directionality of the sugar-phosphate backbones, labeling the 5' and 3' ends with detailed arrows.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain the chemical basis of DNA directionality based on the 5' and 3' carbon positions of deoxyribose.
Define antiparallel orientation and explain why the two strands of the double helix must run in opposite directions.
instructions: Observe the green arrows wrapped around each strand, which indicate direction.
Locate the 5' and 3' text labels at the terminals of both backbones to verify their opposite orientations.

components.text: DNA strands have directionality, designated by 5' (five-prime) and 3' (three-prime) ends. The two strands run in opposite directions. Click and drag to rotate the molecule and examine the directional arrows.

clips.changeMeaning: Add arrows and 5' to 3' labels to highlight the antiparallel orientation of the two strands.
clips.narration: Each strand of DNA has a strict chemical directionality. Look closely at the ends of the backbones: they are designated as five-prime and three-prime, referring to the carbon numbers of the deoxyribose sugar ring. The two strands are antiparallel, meaning they run in opposite directions. One strand runs five-prime to three-prime from top to bottom, while its partner runs three-prime to five-prime. This orientation is essential for base-pairing geometry and replication.

modules.description: An interactive matching puzzle where students drag bases (A, T, G, C) to pair with a 5'-ATGCCAGT-3' template strand, visualizing hydrogen bonds.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply Chargaff's rules of complementary base pairing: Adenine with Thymine, and Guanine with Cytosine.
Differentiate between the double hydrogen bonds of A-T pairs and the triple hydrogen bonds of G-C pairs.
instructions: Drag nitrogenous bases from the tray and align them with their matching base on the template strand.
Observe the formation of two dashed lines for A-T matches and three dashed lines for G-C matches.

components.scriptDescription: Manages the interactive matching puzzle. Detects when user drags base A, T, G, or C onto the complementary strand target spots. If correct, snaps base into position, activates dashed lines for hydrogen bonds (2 for A-T, 3 for G-C) and registers success. If incorrect, rejects with visual feedback.

components.text: Drag base units from the lower palette and dock them onto the empty strand on the right to match the template sequence: 5'-ATGCCAGT-3'. Correct matches will form hydrogen bonds.

clips.changeMeaning: Set up the interactive base-pairing puzzle. One complete template strand is shown, with a palette of loose draggable bases below it.
clips.narration: Now let's practice the complementary base-pairing rules. On your left is a template strand with the sequence: five-prime A, T, G, C, C, A, G, T three-prime. Drag matching nitrogenous bases from the tray below and dock them onto the empty backbone on the right. Remember, Adenine pairs with Thymine, and Guanine pairs with Cytosine. Observe how many hydrogen bonds form for each pair.

modules.description: Introduce the Helicase enzyme as the initial player in replication, physically unwinding the double helix and breaking hydrogen bonds.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: State the biological function of Helicase during DNA replication.
Describe the physical formation of the replication fork as helicase breaks hydrogen bonds and separates the double helix.
instructions: Observe the Helicase enzyme (purple ring) approaching the double helix.
Watch how the hydrogen bonds split apart, leaving two single strands behind the moving enzyme.

components.scriptDescription: Animates the helicase enzyme moving along a linear path, physically splitting a double helix into two separate single-stranded segments behind it.

components.text: Helicase (purple ring) binds to the double helix and moves forward, breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs to separate the two strands, forming a replication fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce Helicase enzyme which separates/unzips the double helix structure.
clips.narration: To replicate DNA, the two strands must first be separated so they can serve as templates. This job belongs to the enzyme Helicase, represented here as a purple ring. Watch as Helicase moves along the double helix, breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the complementary base pairs together. This unzipping action creates the replication fork.

modules.description: Show how Single-Strand Binding Proteins (SSBs) stabilize and hold open the newly exposed single-stranded template strands.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why single-stranded DNA is unstable and explain how SSBs prevent re-annealing.
Differentiate the structural stabilizing role of SSBs from the enzymatically active role of Helicase.
instructions: Observe the orange spherical SSBs binding to both single-stranded templates behind the helicase.
Notice that the template strands remain open and rigid, ready to act as blueprints.

components.text: Single-Strand Binding Proteins (SSBs, orange spheres) quickly coat the exposed strands. They prevent the unstable single strands from re-annealing (snapping back together) or forming secondary structures.

clips.changeMeaning: Add Single-Strand Binding Proteins (SSBs) to the exposed single strands behind the helicase.
clips.narration: Once helicase separates the strands, the exposed bases are highly unstable and prone to snapping back together or twisting into non-functional shapes. Single-Strand Binding Proteins, or SSBs, represented as orange spheres, bind tightly to the single-stranded DNA. They stabilize the exposed templates, keeping them straight and accessible for replication.

modules.description: Show how DNA Polymerase continuously builds the new leading strand in the 5' to 3' direction, following the replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the synthesis directionality of DNA Polymerase (5' to 3' only).
Explain why the leading strand can be synthesized continuously along its 3'-to-5' template strand.
instructions: Watch the blue DNA Polymerase enzyme attach to the left template strand.
Observe how it continuously synthesizes a new complimentary strand (shown in red) right behind the moving replication fork.

components.text: DNA Polymerase III (blue ring) binds to the leading strand template (3' to 5') and continuously adds complementary nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction, following the replication fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Show DNA Polymerase continuously synthesizing the leading strand towards the replication fork.
clips.narration: Now, replication can begin. The enzyme DNA Polymerase III, shown as a large blue ring, is the primary builder. It can only add nucleotides to an existing three-prime end, meaning it synthesizes the new strand in a strict five-prime to three-prime direction. On the leading strand template, which runs three-prime to five-prime into the fork, polymerase can move continuously. It closely follows Helicase, synthesizing a single unbroken complementary strand as the fork opens up.

modules.description: Detail the discontinuous synthesis on the lagging strand template, showing Okazaki fragments and DNA Ligase.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why the lagging strand must be synthesized discontinuously in Okazaki fragments due to the antiparallel layout of DNA.
Identify the molecular role of DNA Ligase in joining Okazaki fragments together by sealing backbones.
instructions: Watch the polymerase on the right strand travel backwards, away from the fork, to create a fragment.
Observe DNA Ligase (green sphere) move along the gaps and seal them together.

components.text: On the lagging strand template (5' to 3'), polymerase must work backward from the fork, creating Okazaki fragments. Watch polymerase build a fragment, jump back, and start another.

clips.changeMeaning: Illustrate the discontinuous synthesis of the lagging strand and formation of Okazaki fragments.
clips.narration: The opposite template strand runs five-prime to three-prime out of the fork, presenting a physical challenge. Since polymerase can only synthesize in the five-prime to three-prime direction, it must work backward, away from the replication fork. It synthesizes a short stretch, detaches, hops back closer to the opening fork, and starts again. This discontinuous synthesis creates a series of segments called Okazaki fragments.

components.text: DNA Ligase (green sphere) acts as glue, forming phosphodiester bonds that seal the nicks between Okazaki fragments, creating a continuous sugar-phosphate backbone.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce DNA Ligase to join the Okazaki fragments into a continuous strand.
clips.narration: To turn these separate fragments into a functional, continuous strand, another enzyme steps in. DNA Ligase, represented here as a green sphere, scans the lagging strand and catalyzes the formation of chemical bonds between the fragments, sealing the gaps. This completes the continuous double-stranded DNA structure.

modules.description: Integrate all replication elements (Helicase, SSBs, Polymerase, and Ligase) into a fully active, unified model of the replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Synthesize understanding of how the different replication enzymes coordinate their tasks at a single replication fork.
Analyze how the physical constraint of antiparallel strands directly forces the asymmetric continuous/discontinuous synthesis styles.
instructions: Rotate the replication fork to view the process from different angles.
Identify each of the five components and observe their roles working in concert.

components.scriptDescription: Drives continuous unified synchronized movement of Helicase, leading Polymerase, lagging Polymerase, SSBs, and Ligase alongside active growth of new leading and lagging DNA strands in the replication fork.

components.text: Now you can observe all 5 replication elements working together in real time. Rotate and zoom in to study how the antiparallel template strands require synchronous leading and lagging strand coordination.

clips.changeMeaning: Activate all five primary components together to show a fully operational replication fork simulation.
clips.narration: Let's see the entire process synchronized. Helicase unwinds at the front, SSBs stabilize the templates, and DNA Polymerase III operates on both strands: continuously on the leading strand, and in fragmented steps on the lagging strand. Finally, DNA Ligase seals the Okazaki fragments. This asymmetric choreography is forced by the antiparallel structure of the double helix.

modules.description: Watch DNA replicate across two generations (gold parental vs silver new strands) and predict daughter molecule composition.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define 'semiconservative' replication and explain why daughter DNA molecules contain one original and one new strand.
Predict the exact ratios of labeled DNA strands after multiple generations of replication.
instructions: Watch the first round of replication where the golden helix splits to form two hybrid gold/silver daughter helices.
Select one of the prediction options on the panel to guess what the next generation will look like.
Observe the second round of replication animation to confirm your hypothesis.

components.scriptDescription: Configures button behavior for multiple-choice quiz questions. Detects selection, communicates with prediction controller, and triggers visual success feedback.
Configures button behavior for multiple-choice quiz questions. Detects selection, communicates with prediction controller, and triggers visual success feedback.
Configures button behavior for multiple-choice quiz questions. Detects selection, communicates with prediction controller, and triggers visual success feedback.

components.text: In replication, each original strand acts as a template. The resulting daughter molecules contain one conserved original strand (gold) and one newly synthesized strand (silver). This is 'semiconservative'.

clips.changeMeaning: Show one round of DNA replication where gold parental strands split and silver new strands are synthesized, creating two hybrid molecules.
clips.narration: DNA replication is called semiconservative. Let's see why. The parental double helix is colored in gold. After one round of replication, the two strands separate and new silver strands are built. The result is two daughter molecules. Each contains one conserved gold strand and one newly-synthesized silver strand. Each daughter has 'conserved' half of the original.

components.text: If these two hybrid (gold/silver) molecules undergo another round of replication in a silver-nucleotide pool, what will the composition of the four resulting molecules be? Choose below.

clips.changeMeaning: Display the prediction question and option buttons for Round 2 of replication.
clips.narration: Now it is your turn to predict. If these two hybrid gold-and-silver daughter molecules undergo a second round of replication using only silver nucleotides, what will the composition of the four resulting double helices be? Look at the options on the panel and select your answer.

components.text: Correct! Round 2 yields 2 hybrid molecules (gold/silver) and 2 fully-new molecules (silver/silver). Semiconservative replication keeps the original strands conserved indefinitely, though they dilute in proportion.

clips.changeMeaning: Disable quiz buttons and play the animation showing the correct outcome of round 2.
clips.narration: That is correct. In the second round of replication, the gold templates are conserved once again, creating two hybrid gold-and-silver molecules, while the silver templates lead to the creation of two entirely silver-silver molecules. This beautiful mechanical tracking was the key insight of the Meselson-Stahl experiment, confirming the semiconservative nature of replication.

modules.description: A final interactive summary screen recapping key conceptual takeaways from the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Consolidate visual and biochemical insights regarding double-helix composition and the steps of DNA replication.
instructions: Read through the summary list.
Observe the slowly rotating DNA double helix model as you review each of the six major concepts.

components.text:
1. Sugar-Phosphate Backbones
2. Complementary Base Pairing (A-T, G-C)
3. Antiparallel 5' to 3' Directionality
4. Replication Fork Enzymes (Helicase, SSBs)
5. Continuous Leading vs. Discontinuous Lagging Strands
6. Semiconservative Nature of Replication

clips.changeMeaning: Provide final summary screen recapping the six core concepts of the DNA lab.
clips.narration: To summarize, we've examined how the structural properties of the double helix dictate its replication. Its antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones and complementary pairing of A to T and G to C provide a perfect molecular blueprint. During replication, enzymes work in an elegant, asymmetric coordination to continuously construct the leading strand and discontinuously assemble the lagging strand, conserving the original sequence for future generations. Thank you for completing this lab!
